Maladaptive Strategies.value: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings
avoid anything that could be stressful
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something about me that made the event happen
My life has been destroyed by the trauma
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: 'Never Alone' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of police violence and the rest of the profile. This item more strongly suggests fear of being alone with a potentially abusive intimate or familiar person, whereas the threat items center on strangers and general vigilance. That mismatch is difficult to explain clinically within the same trauma-linked profile.

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Contamination' is not well aligned with the trauma type and accompanying appraisals. Feeling dirty or contaminated is more characteristic of sexual trauma; with police violence, and with the current memory/threat content, this appraisal stands out as clinically incongruent rather than merely unusual.

vignette: Dr. Thomas Johnson has been a dentist for over three decades, and his practice in a bustling downtown area was once a source of pride and fulfillment. However, his life changed drastically when he experienced an incident involving police violence two years ago. During the event, he was falsely accused of driving under the influence by aggressive officers who brutalized him both physically and verbally before realizing their mistake. Since that day, Thomas has found himself trapped in a vicious cycle of avoidance and heightened vigilance, his mind constantly haunted by memories of the trauma. The memory feels alien to him; it often seems like something that happened to someone else rather than to himself. Yet, when the memory does surface, he vividly hears the harsh commands from the officers and experiences physical pain in the same parts of his body where he was injured. This painful recall has led Thomas to adopt several maladaptive strategies to cope with the overwhelming emotions it evokes. He avoids anything that might trigger these memories or cause any kind of emotional response—whether positive or negative—and constantly scans his environment for signs of potential threats. The belief that something intrinsic about him made the event happen has become deeply ingrained, reinforcing the idea that he is permanently damaged and that life as he knew it is over. Thomas’s fear and hypervigilance have extended into his daily routine. At work, he now always chooses a seat in the dental chair that feels safest from any perceived threat, even though this often disrupts the smooth flow of patient care. He has become so preoccupied with these feelings that he avoids going out alone at night, and his once robust social life has dwindled to almost nothing. His relationship with his partner has also been affected by this heightened state of vigilance. What frightens Thomas most is the constant fear that strangers approaching him in ordinary situations might be a sign of impending danger. This belief is deeply rooted in his negative appraisals, which intensify whenever he relives the trauma through vivid auditory and pain recall. The cycle has become self-reinforcing: as Thomas’s memories grow more intense and alienating, they trigger stronger reactions that drive him further into avoidance and hyper-vigilance. This heightened state of threat monitoring in turn exacerbates his negative appraisals, making him feel even more inherently flawed and trapped by the trauma. Thomas has recently reached a breaking point where the weight of these experiences has become too much to bear alone. He finally decided to seek help out of sheer desperation, hoping that someone could provide him with strategies to break this cycle and regain some semblance of normalcy in his life. What he fears most is being permanently marked by the trauma, unable to escape its shadow. His greatest hope lies in finding a way to reconcile these memories with his identity and reclaim control over his emotional responses.
